title: Demonstrate knowledge of the seed industry

lessons.title: How the seed industry is put together
lessons.html:
From breeder to farmer

Every crop on a South African farm, from a field of maize in Mpumalanga to cabbages near Polokwane, starts with seed. The seed industry is the chain of businesses that develop, produce, check and sell that seed. If you work on a seed farm or in a seed plant, you are one link in this chain.

The main players

  • Plant breeders develop new cultivars that yield more, resist disease or drought, or suit a market better. They work for seed companies, the Agricultural Research Council (ARC) and universities.
  • Seed growers (multipliers) are farmers contracted to grow seed crops. They follow strict rules on isolation, rogueing and harvesting.
  • Seed processors clean, grade, treat, pack and label the seed in a seed plant.
  • Seed testing laboratories test samples for germination, purity, moisture and other qualities.
  • Distributors and retailers such as co-operatives, agri-dealers and seed company agents sell seed to farmers.
  • Farmers, from large commercial producers to smallholders, buy and plant the seed.

Organisations

The South African National Seed Organisation (SANSOR) represents the seed industry and, on behalf of government, runs seed certification schemes for many crops. The national Department of Agriculture is responsible for seed laws, variety listing and official control. Seed companies range from large multinationals to small local businesses that specialise in vegetables, pasture seed or open-pollinated grain.

Main seed markets

By value, hybrid maize is the largest seed market in South Africa, followed by crops such as soybeans, sunflower, wheat and other small grains, sorghum, vegetables and pasture and forage seed. Some seed is also exported to other African countries and further abroad, and some vegetable seed is imported.

Why it matters to you

A farmer only sees the bag. They trust that the seed is the cultivar on the label, that it will germinate, and that it is free of weeds and disease. That trust depends on everyone in the chain, including field workers, plant operators and store staff, doing their work correctly and honestly.

lessons.title: Types of seed, seed classes and certification
lessons.html:
Not all seed is the same

Open-pollinated and hybrid seed

Open-pollinated (OP) cultivars breed true: if you plant seed kept from an OP crop, the next crop looks much like the parent. Hybrid (F1) seed is produced by crossing two selected parent lines. Hybrids often yield more and are very uniform, but seed kept from a hybrid crop does not breed true, so farmers must buy new seed each season. Producing hybrid seed needs careful work, for example detasseling the female rows of maize so they are pollinated only by the male rows.

Genetically modified (GM) seed

Some maize, soybean and cotton cultivars in South Africa are genetically modified, for example for insect resistance or herbicide tolerance. GM crops are regulated under the Genetically Modified Organisms Act and need approval before they are released. Farmers who plant insect-resistant crops must follow the refuge and stewardship requirements on the technology agreement.

Seed classes

Seed is multiplied in steps so that quantity grows while purity is kept:

  1. Breeder seed – a small amount controlled by the breeder.
  2. Pre-basic and basic seed – multiplied from breeder seed under close control.
  3. Certified seed – multiplied from basic seed and sold to farmers for planting.

What certification checks

  • The seed crop was planted with seed of the correct class and cultivar.
  • The field meets isolation distance and previous-crop requirements, to prevent cross-pollination and volunteer plants.
  • Field inspections confirm that off-types, other crops, noxious weeds and diseased plants are within limits; growers remove off-types by rogueing.
  • After processing, samples pass laboratory tests.
  • Bags carry official labels and seals.

Certified seed gives the farmer assurance of cultivar identity and quality. Seed sold outside certification must still meet the legal minimum standards for that crop.

lessons.title: Laws, rights and responsibilities in the seed industry
lessons.html:
Seed is a regulated product

Because farmers cannot see the quality of seed by looking at it, the law sets rules for selling seed.

Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976

This Act and its regulations control the sale of seed and plant material in South Africa. In broad terms it deals with:

  • the official variety list: for most crops only listed cultivars may be sold;
  • registration of seed businesses, such as sellers, packers and cleaners;
  • minimum quality standards for germination and purity;
  • labelling of seed containers with information such as cultivar, lot number, germination and treatment;
  • inspection and sampling by officials.

Plant breeders' rights

Breeding a new cultivar can take ten years or more and cost millions of rand. Plant breeders' rights legislation lets the owner of a new, protected cultivar control who may multiply and sell its seed, much like a patent. Multiplying a protected cultivar without permission is illegal. Seed growers therefore sign contracts that state who owns the seed and that it may only be delivered to the contracting company.

Your responsibilities

  • Keep lots separate and labelled; never mix seed of different lots or cultivars.
  • Report off-types, admixtures or wrong labels immediately.
  • Do not take seed home or give it away; it may be protected and treated with chemicals.
  • Handle treated seed with the PPE on the label and never use it as food or feed.
  • Keep accurate records: they are needed for certification, traceability and complaints.

Seed and food security

Good seed is one of the cheapest inputs per hectare but has the biggest effect on yield. A failed seed lot can cost a farmer a whole season. The seed industry also supports smallholder development through programmes that supply quality seed of suitable cultivars, including open-pollinated cultivars that farmers can save.

Key points

  • The seed chain runs from breeders through growers, processors and laboratories to distributors and farmers.
  • SANSOR runs certification schemes for many crops; the Department of Agriculture regulates seed.
  • Hybrid seed does not breed true, so new seed is bought each season; OP seed can be saved.
  • Certified seed moves from breeder to basic to certified classes with field and lab checks.
  • The Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and plant breeders' rights protect farmers and breeders.
